To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) CS is a novel prognostic marker in men with advanced prostate cancer treated with orchiectomy alone; 2) CS levels in prostatic stroma are associated with overall survival; 3) CS levels in the prostatic stroma of men with metastatic disease are higher than in men with localized disease; and 4) CS levels in peritumoural stroma of men who subsequently relapsed are higher than in those who did not relapse.
CS is increased in the stroma of prostatic biopsies from men with advanced prostate cancer and that CS is a poor predictor of overall survival.
the levels of chondroitinsulphate in the stroma of the prostate gland are elevated in men with advanced prostate cancer and are not associated with the outcome after radical prostatectomy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of CS‐related biomarkers that can be used in the diagnosis of prostate cancer, the prediction of recurrence and the prognosis of disease outcome.
the development of a new class of materials for the treatment of prostate cancer.
the development and evaluation of new methods of diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CS is not an independent predictor of survival outcome in men with advanced prostate cancer.
CS levels in prostatic tissue do not predict survival outcome in patients with advanced disease treated by orchiectomies alone, but they are increased in patients with distant metastases.
the use of a CS‐ELISA assay in conjunction with the PSA‐ELISA is not a useful prognostic tool in men with advanced prostate cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chondroitin sulfates in the stroma of prostate tissue are associated with a more aggressive disease phenotype.
chondroitin sulphate (CS) in the prostate stroma is associated with a poor outcome for men diagnosed with prostate cancer and treated by orchiectomies alone.

CS levels in the stroma surrounding prostate tumors are a useful prognostic factor for predicting recurrence in men with localized prostate cancer, but are not a useful prognosticator of survival in men with metastatic disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
elevated CS levels are associated with metastatic disease and may be a useful marker of advanced prostate cancer.
the level of CS in the prostate does not correlate with overall survival in men with metastatic prostate cancer treated by androgen deprivation.
elevated CS levels were not predictive of survival in this cohort of patients with advanced disease.
